questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Convergence of a Geometric Series With an Arbitrary Starting Index
questions.problem: Which of the following statements is true regarding the series  ${\sum }_{n=3}^{\infty }\frac{2}{15}{(\frac{6}{5})}^{n-1}$ ?
questions.worked_solution:
The series starts with $n=3.$ So the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{3}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{2}{15}{(\frac{6}{5})}^{4-1}}{\frac{2}{15}{(\frac{6}{5})}^{3-1}} \\  & =\frac{{(\frac{6}{5})}^{3}}{{(\frac{6}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the series is divergent because $|r|\ge 1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Range of Values of a Parameter for Which a Geometric Series Converges
questions.problem: For which values of $k$ does the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{kn-2}}{{9}^{n-1}}$ converge?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the series so that it's in the form ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }a{r}^{n},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{kn-2}}{{9}^{n-1}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{kn}\cdot {3}^{-2}}{{9}^{n-1}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{9}(\frac{{3}^{kn}}{{9}^{n-1}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{3}^{kn}}{{9}^{n}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{(\frac{{3}^{k}}{9})}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that this is a geometric series with a common ratio of $r=\frac{{3}^{k}}{9}.$ 

For the series to converge, we require $|r|<1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\frac{{3}^{k}}{9}| & <1 \\ \frac{{3}^{k}}{9} & <1 \\ {3}^{k} & <9.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we could remove the absolute value bars because $\frac{{3}^{k}}{9}$ is always positive.

The equation ${3}^{k}=9$ has the solution $k=2.$ Now, since ${3}^{k}$ increases as $k$ increases, the solution to ${3}^{k}<9$ must be $k<2.$

questions.problem: Which of the following statements is true regarding the series  ${\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(-2){(-0.75)}^{n}$ ?
questions.worked_solution:
The series starts with $n=0.$ So the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{{a}_{0}} \\  & =\frac{(-2){(-0.75)}^{1}}{(-2){(-0.75)}^{0}} \\  & =-0.75.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the series is convergent because $|r|<1.$

questions.problem:
Which of the following geometric series converge?

- $162+108+72+48+⋯$
- $1-\frac{3}{4}+\frac{9}{16}-\frac{27}{64}+⋯$
- $-10-9-8.1-7.29-⋯$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's look at each series in turn.

- For the geometric series $162+108+72+48+⋯$ the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{108}{162} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the series is convergent because $|r|<1.$

- For the geometric series $1-\frac{3}{4}+\frac{9}{16}-\frac{27}{64}+⋯$ the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(-\frac{3}{4})}{1} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the series is convergent because $|r|<1.$

- For the geometric series $-10-9-8.1-7.29-⋯$  the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{-9}{-10} \\  & =0.9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the series is convergent because $|r|<1.$

In conclusion, series I, II, and III converge.

questions.problem:
Find the range of values of $k$ for which the series
${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{(\frac{9}{{81}^{k}})}^{n}$
converges. Do not round the answer.

$k$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
We see that this is a geometric series with a common ratio of $r=\frac{9}{{81}^{k}}.$

For the series to converge, we require $|r|<1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\frac{9}{{81}^{k}}| & <1 \\ \frac{9}{{81}^{k}} & <1 \\ 9 & <{81}^{k} \\ {81}^{k} & >9.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we could remove the absolute value bars because $\frac{9}{{81}^{k}}$ is always positive.

The equation ${81}^{k}=9$ has the solution $k=\frac{1}{2}.$ Now, since ${81}^{k}$ increases as $k$ increases, the solution to ${81}^{k}>9$ must be $k>\frac{1}{2}.$
